title: Insertion sort
learningGoals: trace insertion sort as "take the next card, shift the bigger ones right, drop it in the gap"
write insertion_sort in C with a saved key and a while loop
explain why the key must be saved before shifting
state why insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted data

youtube.title: Insertion Sort = Sorting Playing Cards | C Programming EP 76
youtube.description: You already know this algorithm: it's how you sort cards in your hand. We animate insertion sort on six bars, trace every shift, and write it in C. Plus the bug that overwrites your card before you've saved it. 0:00 Cards in your hand · 0:20 Title · 0:25 The idea · 0:55 Inserting 2, 9 and 1 · 1:45 Inserting 6 and 3 · 2:15 Step trace · 2:40 Code · 3:55 Run it · 4:15 Pun · 4:20 Complexity · 5:00 Bug of the Day · 6:00 Challenge · 6:25 Outro

thumbnail.visual: big text "SORT LIKE CARDS"; a fan of five playing cards with one card lifted and an arrow into a gap; Xecxec holding cards in both claws, smug; Dark blue background, Butter text.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec holding cards in both claws, smug

scenes.onScreen: A hand of cards: 5, 2, 9, 1, 6, 3; Xecxec picks them up one at a time
scenes.animation: Card flick SFX; each card slides into its spot
scenes.narration: You're playing cards at a family get-together. You pick up your cards one at a time. Each new card, you slide into the right place among the cards you're already holding. You've been doing a sorting algorithm your whole life. It's called insertion sort.

scenes.onScreen: Rule card: "Take the next item (key). Shift bigger items right. Drop key in the gap."
scenes.animation: Sorted part on left grows; key lifts above the row
scenes.narration: The left part of the array is your hand, already sorted. At first, the hand is just the first item. Then we take the next item and call it the key. We lift the key out, slide every bigger item in the hand one step right, and drop the key into the gap. Insertion sort doesn't swap pairs. It shifts.

scenes.animation: Key bar lifts in butter; compared bar pastel blue; shifting bar slides right in tomato; key drops into gap; sorted prefix mint; tick per compare, slide SFX per shift, thunk on drop
scenes.narration: Our hand starts as just 5. The key is 2. Is 5 bigger than 2? Yes, so shift 5 right. We've reached the left edge, so drop 2 at the front. Hand: 2, 5. Next key: 9. Is 5 bigger than 9? No. 9 stays where it is. Next key: 1. 9 is bigger, shift. 5 is bigger, shift. 2 is bigger, shift. Left edge: drop 1 at the front. Hand: 1, 2, 5, 9.
Key 6: shift 9, then 5 is smaller, so 6 drops after 5. Key 3: shift 9, shift 6, shift 5, then 2 is smaller, so 3 drops after 2. Sorted.

Here's every step: eleven comparisons and eight shifts. See the moments where a number appears twice, like 5, 5 at step 1.1? That's normal. The key is safely held in a variable, waiting to drop into the gap.

scenes.onScreen: insertion.c (29 lines); tracker for i, key, j, array
scenes.narration: [HL 9] insertion_sort takes the array and its length. [HL 10] i starts at 1, because a hand of one card is already sorted. [TRACK i=1] [HL 11] We save a[i] in key. This line is the most important one. [TRACK key=2] [HL 12] j starts just left of the key. [TRACK j=0] [HL 13] While j is still inside the array and a[j] is bigger than the key, [HL 14] copy a[j] one step right, [TRACK array=5,5,9,1,6,3] [HL 15] and move j left. [TRACK j=-1] The order of the two conditions matters: j greater or equal to 0 is checked first, so we never read a[-1]. That's short-circuit evaluation of the AND operator from Module 2. [HL 17] When the loop stops, j plus 1 is the gap. Drop the key there. [TRACK array=2,5,9,1,6,3] [HL 18] Print the array after each insert. [HL 24] In main, our six cards, [HL 27] and we sort.

code.output:
$ gcc insertion.c -o insertion
$ ./insertion
Insert 2: 2 5 9 1 6 3
Insert 9: 2 5 9 1 6 3
Insert 1: 1 2 5 9 6 3
Insert 6: 1 2 5 6 9 3
Insert 3: 1 2 3 5 6 9

scenes.narration: Compile and run. Insert 2: 2, 5 at the front. Insert 9: no change. Insert 1: it slides all the way to the front. Insert 6, then 3, and we're done.
Why did insertion sort win the card game? It always knew where to put things.

scenes.onScreen: Complexity card; three sorts on our array: bubble 14 compares / 8 swaps, selection 15 / 2, insertion 11 compares / 8 shifts
scenes.narration: In the worst case, a reverse-sorted array, every key shifts past every card in the hand: about n squared over 2 shifts, so O(n²). Average is also O(n²). But the best case is special. If the array is already sorted, each key does one comparison and no shifts, so O(n). Nearly sorted data, like adding a few new marks to a sorted list, is where insertion sort shines. Extra memory: just key, so O(1). And it's stable. On our array: bubble sort 14 comparisons and 8 swaps, selection 15 and 2, insertion 11 comparisons and 8 shifts.

scenes.onScreen: Loop uses cards[i] instead of a saved key; output 5 5 9 9 9 9
scenes.animation: Red siren; key bar gets squashed by the shifting bar, then copies spread
scenes.narration: Today's bug: overwriting before shifting. Someone skipped the key variable and compared with cards[i] directly. But the very first shift writes into cards[i]! The card we were trying to insert is overwritten before we've placed it. The output: 5, 5, 9, 9, 9, 9. Two of our numbers are copied over and over, and 1, 2, 3 and 6 are gone. The fix: save cards[i] in key before the while loop, compare with key, and place key at the end.

Your challenge: write a function insert_sorted that takes a sorted array 10, 20, 40, 50 with room to spare, inserts 30 in the right place, and returns the new length. It's just one pass of insertion sort.
Next episode, we take a break from sorting to understand recursion properly, with a call-stack animation and the Tower of Hanoi. We'll need it for merge sort and quick sort. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
No error or warning from GCC. Wrong output:

5 5 9 9 9 9
bug.why: the first shift writes into cards[i] (because j + 1 == i), destroying the value being inserted, so it must be saved in key first.

pun: Why did insertion sort win the card game? It always knew where to put things.
challenge: Write `int insert_sorted(int a[], int n, int value)` that inserts value into the sorted array a (which has room for one more) and returns the new length. Test: insert 30 into 10 20 40 50.
challengeAnswer: With `int a[10] = {10, 20, 40, 50};` and `n = insert_sorted(a, 4, 30);` the array prints `10 20 30 40 50`.

shorts.title: You already know this algorithm
shorts.hook: "You've been running this algorithm for years."
shorts.script: You pick up playing cards one at a time and slide each one into the right place in your hand. That's a real sorting algorithm with a real name: insertion sort. Here it is, animated and in C.
shorts.caption: Card games taught you DSA.

shorts.title: Insertion sort in 30 seconds
shorts.script: Insertion sort keeps a sorted part on the left. Lift the next item, the key. Shift every bigger item one step right. Drop the key into the gap. Worst case O(n squared). But on data that's already nearly sorted, it's close to O(n), which is why real libraries use it for small or nearly sorted pieces.
shorts.caption: Insertion sort, animated.

shorts.hook: "My sort turned six numbers into two."
shorts.script: This insertion sort compares with cards[i] directly. But the first shift writes over cards[i], so the card we're inserting is destroyed. Output: 5, 5, 9, 9, 9, 9. Fix: save cards[i] into a key variable before you shift anything.
shorts.caption: Save before you shift.

shorts.title: Card game champion
shorts.hook: "Why does insertion sort win at cards?"
shorts.script: Why did insertion sort win the card game? It always knew where to put things.
shorts.caption: Undefeated at family card night.

shorts.title: Insert 30
shorts.hook: "One pass. One number. Where does it go?"
shorts.script: You have 10, 20, 40, 50, sorted. Write a C function that inserts 30 in the right place by shifting, and returns the new length. It's just one pass of insertion sort. Solution pinned on the full episode.
